objectives: Compare changing initial consonants while preserving shared endings.
Use word-family knowledge to support, not replace, complete decoding.
Read controlled short /o/ words and simple text accurately.
concepts: Word families share a recurring ending sound-spelling pattern.
Onsets can change while the rime stays stable.
Automaticity grows through repeated accurate decoding.

definitions.definition: A group of words sharing a common ending sound-spelling pattern.
The initial consonant sound before the vowel and following sounds.
The vowel and following sounds in a syllable, such as -ot or -op.

workedExamples: dog and log share -og; decode the whole word rather than guessing from -og.
commonMistakes: Skipping the full blend because the family is familiar.
keyTakeaways: Use patterns to support accurate reading.
revisionPoints: Shared rime + changing onset = word family.

basic: Sort hot, pot, mop, hop, dog and log by family.
conceptual: Identify the shared rime and changing onset.
higherOrderThinking: Explain why family recognition must not become guessing.
mixedReview: Sort, decode and read a controlled sentence.

mistakeBasedRevision: If the ending is familiar but the word is wrong, return to full decoding.
weakTopicRevision: Decode each family word sound by sound, then reread the family.

outcomes: Learner sorts taught short /o/ words into families with at least 80% accuracy.
Learner identifies shared rime and changing onset.
Learner reads family words accurately without guessing.
Learner reads a controlled sentence and identifies its stated detail.

questions.question: Which word belongs to the -ot family?
Which word belongs to the -op family?
Which word belongs to the -og family?

What changes between hot and pot?
Why are word families useful?
options: They remove the need to blend
They teach every vowel at once

questions.question: When reading a familiar family word, what should the learner still do?
options: Check each grapheme and blend the whole word

questions.question: Which word does NOT belong with hot and pot?
Which word does NOT belong with mop and hop?
Read: “Tom has a mop.” What does Tom have?
What is the main goal of this lesson?
options: Recognize short /o/ word families while maintaining accurate controlled reading
